report_paragraphs: The Genius dataset holds 5,134,856 texts, of which 3,374,198 are tagged as English and 3,233,212 remain after removing the non-song 'misc' tag. A 5% random sample was streamed from the 9 GB file in chunks; after dropping texts shorter than 20 words it contains 161,401 songs. Section headers such as [Chorus] were removed, the text was lower-cased and tokenised, and Genius page views (a true count, G1 = 59.0) were log-transformed (G1 = 0.66).

Songs have a median of 243 words and a median type-token ratio of 0.43; the median song repeats 24% of its lines, which is typical of choruses. Rap lyrics are by far the longest (median 412 words), rock lyrics have the highest vocabulary diversity (median TTR 0.46), and R&B lyrics the lowest (TTR 0.36). The most frequent content words are love, time, want, make, say; the top bigrams are love love, want want, hey hey.

Sentiment was scored on 20,000 songs with VADER and TextBlob. The two agree on the sign for 71.0% of songs and correlate at r = 0.48; VADER spreads scores towards -1 and +1 because long texts accumulate many polar words, whereas TextBlob averages them towards zero. Country is the most positive tag (mean VADER 0.48) and rap the most negative (-0.15).

Joining lyrics to the audio catalogue by normalised title and artist matched 5.9% of the lyric sample. On the 1,202 matched songs, lyric sentiment and audio valence are only weakly related (VADER r = 0.06, TextBlob r = 0.04): a cheerful-sounding track can carry sad words and vice versa, so the two modalities give complementary information.

report_paragraphs: The three automated EDA tools from the course handout were run on the same random sample of 20,000 canonical tracks. YData-Profiling produced a full HTML report in 4.8 s with 10 automatic alerts, including skewness and high-correlation warnings that agree with Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.4. Sweetviz compared the 2,582 tracks from the 1990s with the 8,067 from the 2010s in 6.3 s and visibly showed the shift towards higher energy and lower acousticness. D-Tale started an interactive grid server in 4.1 s and can export pandas code for each operation.

None of the tools knows that a tempo of 0 BPM or a time signature of 0 is impossible, none reports Tukey quartiles or the bias-corrected kurtosis used in the course, and none performs significance tests, dimensionality reduction or time-series decomposition. They are fast first-look tools; the music-specific questions still needed the manual workflow, which is why SonicAtlas embeds the generated reports in its Data Profile page instead of relying on them alone.
